addressed_problems.content: While the study demonstrates the existence of sparse, robust lottery tickets in a small fully-connected model (Lenet 300-100) on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion, the computational expense of iterative pruning combined with adversarial training has so far prevented evaluation on larger architectures (e.g., VGG, ResNet) and more complex vision datasets (e.g., ImageNet). It therefore remains unresolved whether the phenomenon of winning tickets that preserve adversarial robustness generalizes to deeper networks and higher-resolution inputs, and whether the observed trade-offs between sparsity and robustness hold at scale—an open question that directly determines the practical applicability of robust sparse networks in real-world deployment.

The pruning strategies employed in this work produce unstructured sparsity, where individual weights are zeroed out irrespective of the network's architectural structure. Current hardware accelerators and deep-learning libraries, however, are optimized for structured sparsity patterns such as channel-wise or filter-wise pruning. It remains an open problem how to obtain structured sparse, hardware-friendly subnetworks that retain the adversarial robustness observed in the unstructured lottery tickets, without sacrificing the accuracy or robustness gains that magnitude-based iterative pruning provides.

The iterative pruning strategies investigated rely on the strong assumption that weights with the smallest magnitude are the least important for task performance and robustness. This magnitude-based criterion has not been theoretically justified for adversarial robustness, and it is unclear under what conditions it preserves or discards features essential for defending against adversarial perturbations. An open theoretical question is to characterize when and why magnitude-based pruning can identify robust subnetworks, and to develop a principled understanding of the relationship between weight significance and adversarial vulnerability that could guide the design of more reliable pruning algorithms.

The robustness of the found lottery tickets was evaluated only against white-box adversarial attacks (FGSM and PGD). The paper defers to future work the assessment of black-box attacks, which represent a more realistic threat model in many security-critical deployments. It thus remains unresolved whether the sparse, robust subnetworks identified by the lottery ticket hypothesis are also robust to black-box adversaries, and how their robustness compares to dense models under a wider range of attack strengths and perturbation types—a gap that limits confidence in the practical security guarantees of these pruned networks.

The iterative pruning procedure combined with adversarial training is computationally expensive, requiring up to twenty pruning iterations and frequent adversarial example generation every 500 training steps. This computational burden restricts the approach to small models and datasets and hinders broader adoption. It is an open challenge to develop more efficient search procedures—for example, single-shot pruning methods or training schedules that reduce the number of adversarial retraining cycles—that can identify robust sparse subnetworks with significantly lower computational cost while maintaining the robustness and accuracy benefits observed in the iterative lottery ticket approach.

Deep neural networks deployed in vision and embedded settings face two interacting technical bottlenecks. First, large over-parameterized models are expensive in storage and computation, which impedes deployment on resource-limited devices and slows downstream tasks such as formal verification; prior pruning work shows large parameter reductions are possible but leaves open which pruning strategies preserve other desiderata. Second, neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, and prior studies report that higher model capacity tends to improve adversarial robustness, suggesting a possible trade-off between sparsity and robustness. Existing empirical studies that examine sparsity versus robustness either use one-shot or coarse pruning schemes or evaluate pruning and robustness separately; they do not determine whether sparse subnetworks extracted from a dense, randomly-initialized model can themselves be adversarially robust when retrained, nor do they evaluate how different iterative pruning resets (reinitializing to original initialization, reinitializing randomly, or continuing training) affect robustness. As a result, it is unclear (a) whether over-parameterization is necessary to obtain adversarial robustness, (b) which pruning procedures preserve or destroy robustness, and (c) whether sparse, robust subnetworks would be faster to train or more amenable to verification. These gaps prevent principled deployment of compact, verifiable models in security- and safety-critical applications and leave open whether the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (existence of trainable sparse subnetworks due to fortuitous initialization) extends to the adversarial-robustness setting.

nodes.content: In order to deploy robust classifiers in resource-constrained or verifiable settings, practitioners need compact models whose adversarial robustness matches that of large models. Prior to this work, evidence suggested model capacity aids robustness and that pruning tends to reduce robustness, but those studies either used one-shot global pruning or did not examine whether sparsity obtained via the Lottery Ticket iterative procedure preserves adversarial robustness. The unresolved scientific question was: within a randomly-initialized dense network, are there subnetworks (winning tickets) whose fortuitous initializations enable not only competitive natural accuracy but also competitive or improved adversarial robustness after retraining with adversarial examples? Without this knowledge, there is no established procedure to obtain both high robustness and high sparsity simultaneously, preventing reliable compression-for-robustness and hampering verification or deployment of compact robust models.

Even if sparse subnetworks can be made robust, it is important to know whether they retain other desirable training properties such as sample/compute efficiency. Prior work on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis reported that winning tickets can match accuracy using at most the same number of iterations, but it was unknown whether this behavior persists when adversarial training is used (which increases per-iteration cost and can change optimization dynamics). Without empirical evidence on training speed under adversarial objectives, it is unclear whether sparse robust models provide computational advantages in the adversarially-trained regime, which affects their practical value for constrained or time-sensitive training.

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis emphasizes the importance of the original initialization for finding trainable sparse subnetworks, but prior to this work it was unknown whether that emphasis holds under adversarial training and for different pruning-reset strategies. In particular, the scientific gap was whether continuing optimization after pruning (which preserves learned weight structure) could yield greater adversarial robustness than returning to the initial random seed, especially under stronger adversarial objectives (PGD) or on more complex datasets. Resolving this affects algorithm design for producing sparse robust models: if continued training can help robustness, pruning methods should consider learned-weight retention rather than relying solely on initializations.

A practical question for iterative pruning is whether the particular choice of reset rule matters when the target is adversarial robustness. Prior pruning literature used different reset behaviors (reset to original init, reinitialize randomly, or continue training), but their relative effect on adversarial robustness had not been systematically evaluated. If random reinitialization were competitive, it would simplify search; if it is inferior, practitioners must avoid it. The absence of this comparison left an implementation-level uncertainty in designing pruning-for-robustness pipelines.

Many pruning schemes can find reasonably performant subnetworks up to modest compression ratios, but it is scientifically important to identify whether there exists a compression regime where only initialization-aware methods succeed. Prior to this work, the boundary at which initialization begins to dominate—and whether this boundary holds for adversarial robustness as well as natural accuracy—was unclear. Knowing that initialization matters more at extreme sparsity informs both theoretical understanding of why lottery tickets work and practical choices when extreme compression is required for deployment.

To test whether lottery-ticket-style subnetworks can be adversarially robust, a concrete experimental pipeline that couples iterative pruning with adversarial training and compares resetting rules is required. Prior literature lacked a standardized, fully-specified protocol that (a) integrates adversarial-attack generation into each pruning iteration, (b) compares reset strategies under adversarial objectives, and (c) reports hyperparameters and evaluation cadence necessary for reproducibility. Without such a protocol, empirical claims about sparsity-versus-robustness trade-offs are difficult to interpret or reproduce across studies.

Iterative magnitude-based pruning under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (resetting remaining weights to their original random initialization after each pruning iteration) combined with adversarial training using a 50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples yields sparse subnetworks that, when retrained from their original random initializations, achieve higher adversarial test accuracy than the corresponding dense, adversarially-trained network on the MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion datasets. Specifically, on MNIST Digits using a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) with Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) adversarial training (FGSM attack in ℓ^∞ ball with ϵ=0.3) the pruned subnetwork at P_m=16.9% (where P_m is the fraction of weights remaining after pruning) attains FGSM adversarial test accuracy 97.46%±0.16 compared to the dense adversarially-trained model's 94.30%±0.84, and with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial training (PGD attack with 10 iterations, step size α=0.05, in ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3) the same P_m=16.9% subnetwork attains PGD adversarial test accuracy 59.91%±0.81 versus the dense adversarially-trained model's 45.32%±0.20. On MNIST Fashion the pruned subnetwork at P_m=16.9% with PGD adversarial training attains PGD adversarial test accuracy 27.62%±0.97 versus the dense adversarially-trained model's 24.67%±0.71. These numbers demonstrate that robust, sparse subnetworks exist and can exceed the dense model's adversarial robustness at nontrivial sparsity levels.

metadata.narrative: P1 and P2 identify two load‑bearing uncertainties: the 30,000‑iteration evaluation snapshot may systematically favour the sparse subnetwork over the dense model (P1), and the attack parameters used for evaluation are relatively weak, so the measured robustness advantage may not persist under stronger attacks (P2). H1 provides multi‑condition replication that guards against the failure mode of dataset/attack fluke, but does not directly insulate against the biases raised in P1 and P2. The composition is cumulative: P1 and P2 threaten independent aspects (evaluation timing and threat‑model strength), and neither is offset by a highlight that specifically preempts its failure mode. Thus the qualitative existence of robust sparse tickets is reasonably supported by the replicated advantage, but the quantitative superiority claim remains contingent on the evaluation snapshot and the weak threat model. The main risk is that more thorough evaluation (full convergence, stronger attacks) could reduce or reverse the claimed advantage.

nodes.title: Existence of sparse, adversarially-robust subnetworks via iterative magnitude pruning with adversarial training

nodes.content: Sparse subnetworks identified by the Lottery Ticket iterative magnitude-pruning procedure (iterative pruning with resetting of remaining weights to their original random initialization after each pruning iteration) combined with adversarial training (50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples) reach the early-stopping criterion (minimum validation loss) in fewer training iterations than the original dense network (the unpruned model with 100% of weights), indicating faster apparent convergence, and they maintain comparable natural (clean-image) accuracy at those stopping points. Across the MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion datasets using a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) with adversarial training using either Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) (in ℓ^∞ ball with ϵ=0.3) or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) (10 iterations, step size α=0.05, ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3) attacks, early-stopping iteration curves (adversarial validation loss vs. training iteration) show that at many pruning levels the winning tickets stop earlier and their natural validation accuracies at early stop are similar to or exceed the dense baseline.

metadata.narrative: No load‑bearing weak points were identified; the early‑stopping advantage and maintained natural accuracy are directly observable from the reported learning curves. H2 confirms that the pattern holds across two datasets and two attack types, providing generalization support that precludes the failure mode of dataset/attack specificity. The conclusion rests on direct measurement and is underwritten by the multi‑condition replication.

nodes.title: Sparse subnetworks with adversarial training reach early-stopping criterion earlier than dense network while maintaining natural accuracy

nodes.content: When using continued-training pruning (never resetting remaining weights after each pruning iteration, continuing to train the current parameter set), the resulting pruned networks can outperform the Lottery Ticket resetting strategy (resetting remaining weights to their original random initialization after each pruning iteration) in adversarial robustness for stronger attacks (Projected Gradient Descent, PGD) and more complex scenarios. Specifically, in the MNIST Digits experiments with PGD adversarial training (PGD attack: 10 iterations, step size α=0.05, ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3) on a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters), the continued-training strategy shows higher adversarial test accuracy at P_m=51.3% (where P_m is the fraction of weights remaining after pruning) in comparison to the original reset-to-initialization lottery ticket strategy; similarly, in MNIST Fashion with PGD the most robust model observed occurs at P_m=16.9% under continued training. This demonstrates that for stronger adversaries (PGD) and harder datasets (MNIST Fashion), retaining learned weights across pruning iterations can produce more robust sparse models than reinitializing to the original random weights.

metadata.narrative: P3 identifies a statistical weak point: the evidence for continued training’s superiority at specific sparsity levels (51.3% on Digits, 16.9% on Fashion under PGD) rests on visual inspection of plots whose error bars overlap, without tabulated numerical comparisons or significance tests. The conclusion’s comparative claim is therefore weakly supported; it is possible that the observed advantage is within measurement noise. No highlight offsets this uncertainty. The conclusion should be treated as an exploratory observation requiring confirmation with stronger statistical evidence rather than a robust empirical finding.

nodes.title: Continued-training pruning can outperform lottery-reset pruning in adversarial robustness for stronger attacks and harder datasets

nodes.content: Iterative pruning that reinitializes the remaining weights to fresh random draws from the initialization distribution at each pruning iteration (the "random reinitialization" strategy) is empirically outperformed by at least one of the other evaluated strategies (original lottery-reset: resetting remaining weights to their original random initialization; continued training: never resetting weights) in all experiments on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion using a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) with adversarial training using either Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) (in ℓ^∞ ball with ϵ=0.3) or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) (10 iterations, step size α=0.05, ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3). The adversarial test accuracy and early-stopping iteration values for the random strategy are consistently lower (for test accuracy) or higher (for early-stopping iteration, indicating slower convergence) than the better-performing alternative across all pruning levels.

metadata.narrative: No load‑bearing weak points were identified. H3 confirms that the dominance of random reinitialization by at least one of the other strategies holds across all tested conditions (both datasets, both attacks, all sparsity levels), providing a comprehensive empirical boundary. The conclusion is a direct comparative observation from the reported plots and is well‑supported by the breadth of evidence.

nodes.title: Random reinitialization pruning is outperformed by original or continued-training strategies in adversarial robustness

nodes.content: At sparsity levels P_m=3.6% and P_m=1.8% (where P_m is the fraction of weights remaining after pruning, corresponding to pruning 96.4% and 98.2% of weights), subnetworks found by the Lottery Ticket iterative-reset procedure (iterative pruning with resetting of remaining weights to their original random initialization after each pruning iteration) consistently outperform the alternative pruning strategies (random reinitialization and continued training) in natural and adversarial accuracy on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion using a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) with adversarial training using either Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) (in ℓ^∞ ball with ϵ=0.3) or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) (10 iterations, step size α=0.05, ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3). This demonstrates that fortuitous initializations are especially critical for successful retraining at extreme compression, as the original lottery-reset strategy yields higher average adversarial and natural test accuracies than random reinitialization or continued-training baselines across these trials.

metadata.narrative: P4 points out that the claim of consistent outperformance at extreme sparsities (3.6%, 1.8%) is based on visual comparisons in line plots rather than tabulated numerical comparisons; the differences may be small relative to noise. H4 provides independent weight‑distribution evidence that the surviving initializations are non‑uniformly selected, supporting the mechanistic attribution to initialization and partially countering the concern that the accuracy differences are noise. However, H4 does not directly address the statistical significance of the accuracy differences; it operates on a different layer (mechanism vs. quantitative comparison). Thus the composition is partially offsetting: H4 increases confidence that initialization matters at extreme sparsity, but the specific quantitative claim that winning tickets ‘constantly outperform’ remains under‑supported by direct accuracy statistics. The conclusion’s qualitative direction (initialization matters more at extreme sparsity) is plausible, but the claim of quantitative superiority requires stronger tabulated evidence.

nodes.title: Lottery-ticket resetting strategy outperforms alternatives at extreme sparsity levels

nodes.content: A reproducible experimental protocol was defined and executed: three iterative pruning strategies (original lottery-reset: resetting remaining weights to θ_0~D_θ, where D_θ denotes the distribution of initial parameters; random reinitialization: resetting remaining weights to fresh random draws θ_0'~D_θ; and continued training: never resetting weights) were evaluated in combination with adversarial training using Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks. The experimental configuration used a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10; total 266,200 trainable parameters), no biases, ReLU activations in hidden layers, Adam optimizer with learning rate 1.2×10^{-3}, batch size 60, training for 50,000 iterations per pruning iteration, pruning iterations repeated for up to 20 iterations, pruning rates of 20% for the first two layers and 10% for the output layer per pruning iteration, FGSM crafted in an ℓ^∞ ball with ϵ=0.3, PGD crafted with 10 iterations and step size α=0.05 within ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3, adversarial training using a 50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples, evaluation on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion with 5 trial averages, and model evaluation on natural and adversarial validation and test sets every 500 training iterations. This protocol operationalizes the combination of Lottery Ticket-style iterative pruning with adversarial objectives and provides a baseline suite for future comparisons.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion describes the experimental protocol that was executed; it is a statement of method rather than an empirical discovery. No load‑bearing weak points or distinguishing strengths were identified. The protocol is reported in sufficient detail to be reproducible, and no uncertainties threaten its description.

nodes.title: Reproducible experimental protocol for iterative pruning with adversarial training

nodes.content: In the experiments on the Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) trained with adversarial training (50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples generated by either Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) with ϵ=0.3 or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) with step size 0.05 for 10 iterations within ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3, Adam optimizer, learning rate 1.2e-3, batch size 60) on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion, the adversarial test accuracy comparisons between the dense adversarially-trained model (100% sparsity, i.e., zero pruning) and the pruned subnetworks at various sparsity levels (e.g., 16.9% remaining weights, where P_m denotes the fraction of weights remaining) are reported after 30,000 training iterations within the current training cycle. This fixed evaluation point may systematically favour the pruned subnetwork because the dense model's adversarial accuracy continues to improve beyond 30,000 iterations (the total training cycle is 50,000 iterations), while the pruned subnetwork converges to near-peak accuracy earlier in training (as indicated by reaching the early-stopping criterion of minimum validation loss in fewer iterations compared to the dense model).Table 1 (footnote: after 30,000 training iterations); Fig. 1, Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the 30,000‑iteration evaluation point does indeed systematically favour the sparse subnetwork because the dense model has not yet converged, then the reported quantitative advantage of the sparse subnetwork over the dense model (e.g. +14.59 percentage points on MNIST Digits PGD) may be artificially inflated or even reversed at full convergence. The conclusion that sparse subnetworks ‘achieve higher adversarial test accuracy than the corresponding dense, adversarially‑trained network’ would need to be restricted to the 30,000‑iteration snapshot, unless convergence‑level comparisons are provided.

refs.text: Table 1 (footnote: after 30,000 training iterations); Fig. 1, Fig. 2

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper trains models for 50,000 iterations per pruning cycle but evaluates at 30,000 iterations uniformly. The choice of 30,000 is not justified by convergence checks; the dense model’s learning curve may not have plateaued by that point. If early‑stopping behaviour differs (sparse converge faster), comparing at a fixed early iteration inflates the apparent advantage of sparser models. Standard practice for comparing final accuracy is to evaluate at convergence or after the same number of training steps from initialization, but the dense and sparse models have different total training histories (dense has only one training cycle, sparse subnetworks have undergone multiple prune‑and‑retrain cycles, with weights reset to original init each time), making the interpretation of ‘30,000 iterations into the current cycle’ asymmetric.

nodes.title: Fixed evaluation at 30,000 iterations may advantage pruned subnetworks due to their faster convergence

nodes.content: In the Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) trained with adversarial training (50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples) using either Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) or Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion, with FGSM attack parameters: ϵ=0.3 in ℓ^∞ ball, PGD attack parameters: step size α=0.05, 10 iterations, within ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3, the adversarial test accuracy used to support the claim that sparse subnetworks are robust is measured only against the same type of white-box attack used during training, with fixed hyperparameters. Stronger adversarial attacks (e.g., PGD with 40 iterations, multiple random restarts, or black-box attacks) are not evaluated.Section 2.3.2 (PGD definition), Section 4.2 (attack hyperparameters)

metadata.failure_mode: If the threat model used for evaluation (FGSM or 10‑step PGD with epsilon=0.3) is not sufficiently strong to distinguish truly robust models from partially robust ones, then the adversarial test accuracy advantage of the sparse subnetwork over the dense model may be an artifact of the weak attack. Under a stronger attack (e.g. PGD with 40 steps and 10 random restarts), the dense model might prove more robust than the sparse subnetwork, reversing the conclusion’s claimed superiority. At minimum, the conclusion would need to be qualified as applying only to the specific, relatively weak attack parameters used.
metadata.weakness_reason: The adversarial robustness literature (e.g. Madry et al. 2017) establishes that PGD with 10 iterations is often insufficient to approximate the optimal perturbation, and that robust accuracy typically degrades under more iterations or random restarts. The paper’s own attacks are relatively weak (epsilon=0.3 is moderate, 10 PGD steps is low). Without evaluation against a stronger adversary, the reported accuracy numbers may overstate the true robustness of the subnetworks. The paper acknowledges this as future work, but the conclusion’s claim of ‘robustness’ lacks a quantifiable bound against a stronger threat model.

nodes.title: Adversarial robustness measured only against same attack type used during training with fixed hyperparameters

nodes.content: In the comparison between continued-training pruning (never resetting remaining weights after each pruning iteration) and original lottery‑reset pruning (resetting remaining weights to their original random initialization after each pruning iteration) under Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial training on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion using a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) with PGD attack parameters: step size 0.05, 10 iterations, within ℓ^∞ ball ϵ=0.3, trained with Adam optimizer, learning rate 1.2e-3, batch size 60, 50,000 iterations per pruning iteration, adversarial training with 50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples, the claim that continued training yields higher adversarial test accuracy at certain sparsity levels (specifically, at P_m=51.3% on Digits and P_m=16.9% on Fashion, where P_m is the fraction of weights remaining after pruning) is supported only by visual examination of the adversarial test accuracy vs. training iteration plots. Numerical values of adversarial test accuracy at those sparsity levels for both strategies are not reported in a table, and the error bars (standard deviations over 5 trials) shown on the plots overlap at many training iterations, making it unclear whether the observed advantage exceeds the measurement noise.Fig. 2, Fig. 8

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed advantage of continued training at those sparsity levels is within the statistical noise (i.e. not reproducible), then Conclusion 3 would be unsupported: there would be no evidence that continued training ‘sometimes yields higher robustness’ beyond random variation. The claim that continued training outperforms lottery‑reset under strong attacks would need to be withdrawn or tightened to a weaker statement of exploratory observation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper presents line plots with error bars but does not provide a direct numerical comparison (e.g. a table of mean accuracies and standard deviations at a fixed evaluation point) for the specific sparsity levels where continued training appears superior. Overlapping error bars in time‑series plots are visually ambiguous; without a quantitative statement, the reader cannot assess effect size or significance. The paper’s own discussion acknowledges that this occurs only in ‘specific scenarios’, but the strength of evidence for those scenarios is not statistically established.

nodes.title: Claim of continued-training advantage at specific sparsity levels lacks numerical table verification and has overlapping error bars

nodes.content: In the evaluation of pruning strategies at extreme sparsity levels (P_m=3.6% and P_m=1.8%, where P_m is the fraction of weights remaining after pruning, corresponding to 96.4% and 98.2% pruning) on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion under Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial training with the Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron (MLP) (three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, 10, ReLU activations, no biases, 266,200 trainable parameters) and hyperparameters: FGSM attack ϵ=0.3 in ℓ^∞ ball, PGD attack with step size 0.05, 10 iterations, ϵ=0.3, Adam optimizer, learning rate 1.2e-3, batch size 60, 50,000 iterations per pruning iteration, adversarial training with 50/50 split, the claim that the original lottery‑reset strategy (resetting remaining weights to their original random initialization at each pruning iteration) consistently outperforms all other approaches (random reinitialization and continued training) in adversarial and natural accuracy is based on visual comparison of the adversarial test accuracy vs. training iteration plots for the three strategies at these sparsity levels rather than on tabulated numerical comparisons with error bars specific to those extreme sparsities. The differences in adversarial test accuracy between strategies at these sparsity levels appear small in the plots, and the error bars (standard deviations over 5 trials) may overlap, particularly at the P_m=1.8% level.Figs. 1, 2, 7, 8

metadata.failure_mode: If the differences between pruning strategies at extreme sparsity are within the measurement noise and not statistically significant, then Conclusion 5—that winning tickets remain superior at extreme sparsity—would be unsupported. The assertion that ‘fortuitous initializations are especially critical for successful retraining at extreme compression’ would lose its empirical foundation, reducing the claim to a plausible but unconfirmed hypothesis.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not provide a dedicated table or annotation showing the exact mean and standard deviation of adversarial test accuracy for each pruning strategy at the extreme sparsity levels, nor does it perform a statistical test of the null hypothesis that the strategies have equal mean accuracy. Given that the total number of remaining parameters is very small (e.g. at 1.8% sparsity, about 4,800 parameters), the model’s performance is highly variable; the observed advantage of the original strategy may be within the noise of the 5‑trial average. The claim of superiority requires stronger quantitative evidence than visual inspection.

nodes.title: Extreme-sparsity superiority claim of lottery-reset strategy lacks tabulated numerical support and may have overlapping error bars

nodes.content: Across the reported experiments on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion with the Lenet 300‑100 MLP trained adversarially (FGSM and PGD), the sparse subnetwork at 16.9% sparsity (83.1% of weights pruned) obtained by iterative magnitude pruning with reset to original initialization achieves consistently higher adversarial test accuracy than the dense adversarially‑trained baseline under both attack types and on both datasets: on MNIST Digits, +3.16 percentage points (97.46% vs 94.30%) under FGSM, +14.59 percentage points (59.91% vs 45.32%) under PGD; on MNIST Fashion, +2.95 percentage points (27.62% vs 24.67%) under PGD (the FGSM comparison is similar in direction but smaller). The improvement is not an isolated single‑condition observation but replicates across four distinct conditions differing in dataset and attack type.

metadata.credit: The replication across two datasets and two attack types precludes the failure mode where the advantage is a fluke of a single experimental setting (e.g. specific dataset artifacts or attack parameter choices). Without this replication, a reader could dismiss the result as dataset‑ or attack‑specific. The consistent direction and non‑trivial magnitude across multiple conditions provide substantive support for the qualitative conclusion that robust sparse subnetworks exist: the improvement is not limited to one narrow configuration. The credit is that the qualitative direction of the conclusion (existence of sparse subnetworks with adversarial accuracy at or above the dense baseline) is underwritten at the layer of qualitative direction across the tested regime; the quantitative magnitudes vary by condition, but the replicability reduces the risk that the observation is an experimental artifact.

nodes.title: Multi‑condition replication of sparse‑subnetwork superiority

nodes.content: For the Lenet 300‑100 MLP adversarially trained (FGSM and PGD) on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion, the early‑stopping iteration (training iteration at which minimum validation loss is reached) for sparse subnetworks found by the original lottery‑reset pruning strategy is consistently lower than that of the dense model across multiple sparsity levels, and their natural (clean‑image) validation accuracy at that early‑stopping point is equal to or higher than the dense model’s natural validation accuracy at its own early‑stopping point. This pattern holds for both datasets and both attack types, as shown in the early‑stopping validation accuracy plots (Figures 3, 5, 9, 11).

metadata.credit: The early‑stopping advantage and preserved natural accuracy are replicated across four distinct experimental settings (two datasets × two attack types), precluding the failure mode that the training speed improvement is due to idiosyncratic properties of a single dataset or attack. The consistent pattern—sparse tickets stop earlier without sacrificing natural accuracy—provides a quantitative behavioural invariant that supports the conclusion that sparse robust tickets train faster while maintaining natural accuracy. Without this multi‑condition replication, the claim would rest on a single dataset‑attack pair and be vulnerable to the objection that the observed speedup is dataset‑specific (e.g. MNIST Digits being too easy). The replication across MNIST Fashion establishes that the result extends beyond the simpler digit‑recognition task to a more complex (clothing) classification problem.

nodes.title: Multi‑condition replication of early‑stopping advantage

nodes.content: In the systematic comparison of three iterative pruning strategies (reset to original initialization, random reinitialization, continued training) under adversarial training (FGSM and PGD) on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion with the Lenet 300‑100 MLP, the random reinitialization strategy yields adversarial test accuracy curves that are consistently lower than at least one of the other two strategies at every reported sparsity level and across both datasets and both attack types, as shown in Figures 1, 2, 7, 8.

metadata.credit: The comprehensive nature of the comparison—spanning two datasets, two attack types, and all sparsity levels from 51.3% down to 1.8%—provides strong evidence that random reinitialization is dominated without exception, precluding the failure mode where a systematic advantage could appear in a specific unexplored regime. This underwrites the conclusion’s comparative claim at the level of qualitative ordering across the entire evaluated experimental space. Without this multi‑condition consistency, a practitioner might still entertain random reinitialization as a viable strategy for certain attack/sparsity combinations; the evidence here rules it out uniformly for the tested configurations.

nodes.title: Comprehensive empirical dominance of random reinitialization

nodes.content: For the Lenet 300‑100 MLP trained on MNIST Digits under normal, FGSM‑adversarial, and PGD‑adversarial training, the weight distributions of the surviving parameters in winning tickets (original lottery‑reset strategy) at sparsity levels 51.3%, 16.9%, 8.7%, 3.6%, and 1.8% (Figures 13, 14, 15) show that the surviving initializations are not uniformly distributed across the parameter range but concentrate near specific values (e.g. the first hidden layer’s distribution peaks near zero while the second and output layers have broader, offset peaks). This structured pattern differs from what would be expected if the mask were random, providing independent evidence that the original initialization matters for the lottery ticket’s retrainability.

metadata.credit: The weight‑distribution histograms provide a mechanistic layer of evidence that goes beyond the accuracy comparisons: they show that the pruning process selects weights with particular initialization values, consistent with the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis claim that fortuitous initializations are causally responsible for the superior retrainability of winning tickets. If the histograms showed uniform distributions (no selection bias), the superiority at extreme sparsity would lack a mechanistic explanation and could be attributed to other factors (e.g. lower effective capacity reducing overfitting). By showing non‑uniform selection, the paper supplies supportive evidence for the causal mechanism, strengthening the conclusion that winning tickets remain superior at extreme sparsity because of initialization, not merely because of reduced parameter count. The scope of credit is partial: the histograms support the mechanistic attribution but do not confirm it definitively (confounds remain), so the conclusion’s quantitative accuracy comparisons receive indirect support from this independent check.

nodes.title: Weight‑distribution evidence for initialization‑driven selection

steps.reasoning: Treat the experimental protocol defined earlier (the iterative pruning strategies, model, adversarial attacks, training hyperparameters, dataset splits, and evaluation cadence) as given; this protocol is used to obtain the results presented in tables and figures that support the existence claim. (Refer to the protocol conclusion as established and the definitions of $P_{m}$, adversarial training split, FGSM, and PGD as specified.)

Explain what it means for a subnetwork to be a "winning ticket" in this work's context: a winning ticket is a subnetwork obtained by iterative magnitude-based pruning (pruning smallest-magnitude weights per the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis iterative-reset procedure), represented by a mask $m$ with sparsity $P_{m}=\frac{\|m\|_0}{|\theta|}$, and then retrained from its original random initialization values $\theta_0\sim\mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ under adversarial training (50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples).

Present the MNIST Digits evidence measured under the FGSM adversary: Table 1 reports test accuracies after 30,000 training iterations for the Lenet 300-100 model pruned by the iterative Lottery Ticket approach; for $P_{m}=16.9\%$ the FGSM adversarial test accuracy value shown for the adversarially-trained pruned subnetwork is $97.46\%\pm 0.16$, while the dense adversarially-trained model's FGSM adversarial test accuracy is $94.30\%\pm 0.84$ as reported in the same table, demonstrating the pruned subnetwork outperforms the dense model under FGSM.
Table 1
[6]

Present the MNIST Digits evidence measured under the PGD adversary: Table 1 reports for $P_{m}=16.9\%$ that the adversarially-trained pruned subnetwork achieves PGD adversarial test accuracy $59.91\%\pm 0.81$, while the dense adversarially-trained model's PGD adversarial test accuracy is $45.32\%\pm 0.20$, showing the pruned subnetwork also outperforms the dense model under the stronger PGD attack.
Table 1
[14]

Present the MNIST Fashion evidence measured under PGD adversary: Table 2 reports for $P_{m}=16.9\%$ that the adversarially-trained pruned subnetwork achieves PGD adversarial test accuracy $27.62\%\pm 0.97$, whereas the dense adversarially-trained model's PGD adversarial test accuracy is $24.67\%\pm 0.71$, indicating the pruned subnetwork outperforms the dense baseline on MNIST Fashion under PGD as well.
Table 2
[14]

Point to temporal/per-iteration evidence that these pruned subnetworks are robust during training as well: Figures showing adversarial test accuracy over training iterations (Figure 1 for FGSM and Figure 2 for PGD) include curves for various $P_{m}$ values and show that curves for the pruned winning-ticket masks exhibit higher adversarial test accuracy than the dense adversarially-trained baseline across training, supporting that retrained winning tickets maintain superior adversarial robustness not only at final evaluation but across training.
Fig. 1,Fig. 2

Note the experimental averaging and statistical reporting that support these numerical comparisons: reported numbers in Tables 1 and 2 are averages over five independent trials and include standard deviations, and the claimed improvements are observed in these averaged results with the stated standard deviations, providing quantitative evidence for the existence of robust sparse subnetworks at the reported sparsities and attacks.
Table 1,Table 2

Conclude from the foregoing data that iterative magnitude-based pruning under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, when combined with adversarial training (50/50 split of natural and adversarial examples) and retraining the pruned subnetwork from its original random initialization $\theta_0$, yields sparse subnetworks that, in the reported MNIST experiments, achieve higher adversarial test accuracy than the corresponding dense adversarially-trained network at the reported $P_{m}$ values; therefore robust, sparse subnetworks exist and can exceed dense-model adversarial robustness at nontrivial sparsity levels.
Table 1,Table 2,Fig. 1,Fig. 2

Treat the protocol conclusion as established (iterative pruning strategies, training hyperparameters, evaluation cadence) and adopt the paper's definition of early-stopping used in experiments: early-stopping iteration is defined as the training iteration that minimizes validation loss (minimum adversarial validation loss is used as the early-stopping criterion in adversarial experiments).

State the empirical measurement performed to assess training speed: for each pruning strategy and sparsity level $P_{m}$ the authors record the iteration at which the minimum validation loss occurs (the early-stopping iteration) and report the adversarial and natural validation accuracies at that stopping point; these curves are averaged over five trials and plotted.

Present MNIST Digits FGSM evidence: Figure 3 contains three panels for Lenet 300-100 on MNIST Digits under FGSM adversarial training — left panel shows early-stopping iteration as a function of $P_{m}$, middle panel shows adversarial accuracy at early stop, right panel shows natural accuracy at early stop; in the left panel many winning-ticket curves corresponding to pruned $P_{m}$ values lie below the dense baseline curve, indicating the pruned subnetworks reach the early-stopping criterion in fewer training iterations than the dense network; the middle and right panels show that adversarial and natural validation accuracies at these earlier stopping points are similar to or exceed the dense baseline.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Present MNIST Digits PGD evidence: Figure 5 presents analogous plots for PGD adversarial training; the left panel again shows that many pruned winning-ticket curves reach the early-stopping criterion earlier (fewer training iterations) than the dense baseline; the adversarial and natural accuracies at those early stops (middle and right panels) remain comparable to or exceed the dense baseline, demonstrating pruned subnetworks maintain accuracy while training in fewer iterations.
Fig. 5

Present MNIST Fashion supporting evidence: Supplementary Figures 9 and 11 (MNIST Fashion FGSM and PGD respectively) show the same pattern for the Fashion dataset — pruned winning tickets at many $P_{m}$ values have earlier early-stopping iterations and adversarial/natural accuracies at early stop comparable to or exceeding the dense baseline — reinforcing that the observed faster apparent convergence generalizes across both datasets considered.
Fig. 9,Fig. 11

Report statistics and averaging that support the claim: the curves and reported early-stopping data are averages across five trials with error bars representing standard deviation, and the consistent trend of lower early-stopping iterations across multiple pruning levels indicates a reproducible pattern where winning tickets require fewer training iterations under the adversarial training regimes evaluated while preserving natural accuracy at the stopping point.

Conclude that iterative-magnitude-pruned subnetworks identified by the Lottery Ticket procedure with adversarial training reach the early-stopping criterion in fewer training iterations than the original dense network and maintain comparable natural accuracy at those stopping points across the reported MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion experiments.
Fig. 3,Fig. 5,Fig. 9,Fig. 11

Treat the experimental protocol conclusion as established and recall that PGD is a stronger, multi-step adversary compared to FGSM as defined earlier; PGD was used with $10$ iterations and step size $\alpha=0.05$ within $\ell^{\infty}$ ball $\epsilon=0.3$ in these experiments.
[14]

Explain the comparison of reset strategies: the three iterative pruning strategies (original lottery-reset to $\theta_0$, random reinitialization, continued training) are compared in terms of adversarial test accuracy as training proceeds for various sparsity levels $P_{m}$, and these comparisons are visualized in the figures that plot adversarial test accuracy curves for each strategy and $P_{m}$.

Present MNIST Digits PGD evidence: Figure 2 (Lenet 300-100 on MNIST Digits with PGD) shows adversarial test-accuracy curves for different $P_{m}$ values and includes comparisons between the original-reset strategy and the continued-training strategy; in that figure the continued-training curves at $P_{m}=51.3\%$ lie above the corresponding original-reset curves in adversarial test accuracy, indicating that for $P_{m}=51.3\%$ under PGD adversarial training the continued-training pruning strategy yields higher adversarial robustness than the lottery-reset strategy.
Fig. 2

Present MNIST Fashion PGD evidence: Figure 8 (Lenet 300-100 on MNIST Fashion with PGD, Supplementary) shows adversarial test-accuracy comparisons across strategies; the authors report that the most robust model observed on MNIST Fashion under PGD occurs at $P_{m}=16.9\%$ using the continued-training strategy, i.e., continued training produced the highest adversarial test accuracy at that sparsity level compared to original-reset and random reinitialization.
Fig. 8

Provide the paper's qualitative interpretation linking the phenomenon to problem difficulty and attacker strength: the authors note that PGD is a stronger adversary than FGSM and that in "more complex scenarios" (e.g., MNIST Fashion or under PGD) retaining learned weights across pruning iterations can produce more robust sparse models than reinitializing to original random weights, suggesting the benefit of continued training becomes apparent under stronger attacks or harder datasets.
[6]

Conclude that, based on the plotted adversarial test-accuracy comparisons under PGD, there exist cases (notably MNIST Digits at $P_{m}=51.3\%$ and MNIST Fashion at $P_{m}=16.9\%$) where continued-training pruning produces pruned networks with higher adversarial robustness than the Lottery Ticket reset-to-initialization strategy; therefore continued-training can sometimes outperform lottery-reset under strong adversaries and more complex datasets.
Fig. 2,Fig. 8

Treat the protocol conclusion as established and recall the definition of the "random reinitialization" strategy: after each prune step the remaining weights are reinitialized to fresh random samples $\theta_0'\sim\mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ prior to the next training phase.

Summarize the empirical comparisons across strategies: Figures that plot adversarial test accuracy over training for different $P_{m}$ values (Figure 1 for FGSM on MNIST Digits, Figure 2 for PGD on MNIST Digits, and Supplementary Figures 7 and 8 for MNIST Fashion FGSM and PGD respectively) include curves for the random-reinitialization strategy alongside the original-reset and continued-training curves; these plots show the random strategy's curves consistently lie below at least one of the other strategies across pruning levels.
Fig. 1,Fig. 2,Fig. 7,Fig. 8

Report the paper's textual summary: the Discussion explicitly states that "it is important to note that the random reinitialization pruning technique is outperformed by at least one of the other approaches in all cases," which is the authors' assessment that across the experiments the random strategy is never strictly superior and is empirically dominated by either original-reset or continued-training in adversarial test accuracy and early-stopping behavior.

Conclude that iterative pruning with random reinitialization is empirically outperformed by at least one of the other evaluated strategies (original lottery-reset or continued training) across the reported MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion experiments with FGSM and PGD adversarial training, and therefore the random strategy is dominated by the alternatives in these experiments.
Fig. 1,Fig. 2,Fig. 7,Fig. 8

Treat the protocol conclusion as established and recall the definition of extreme sparsity levels: $P_{m}$ denotes the fraction of weights remaining; thus $P_{m}=3.6\%$ corresponds to pruning $96.4\%$ of parameters and $P_{m}=1.8\%$ corresponds to pruning $98.2\%$ of parameters.

Present the absolute performance of winning tickets at extreme sparsity from reported tables: Table 1 (MNIST Digits) reports, for example, that at $P_{m}=3.6\%$ the adversarially-trained pruned network under FGSM attains adversarial test accuracy $95.23\%\pm 0.75$ and under PGD attains adversarial test accuracy $48.81\%\pm 0.98$, and at $P_{m}=1.8\%$ the FGSM adversarial accuracy is $90.15\%\pm 1.45$ and PGD adversarial accuracy is $38.23\%\pm 2.33$, showing that the original lottery-reset winners retain substantial adversarial and natural accuracy even at these extreme compression levels.
Table 1

Present MNIST Fashion extreme-sparsity performance from reported tables: Table 2 reports that at $P_{m}=3.6\%$ and $P_{m}=1.8\%$ the adversarially-trained pruned networks retain notably high natural test accuracy relative to more heavily pruned baselines (e.g., $87.13\%\pm 0.25$ natural at $P_{m}=3.6\%$ and $85.70\%\pm 0.20$ at $P_{m}=1.8\%$ under FGSM adversarial training), which demonstrates that the winning-ticket pruning procedure yields usable models even at extreme sparsities.
Table 2

Point to cross-strategy comparisons and initialization evidence: the Discussion states that winning lottery tickets "constantly outperform all other approaches at the highest level of sparsity of 3.6% and 1.8%," and Supplementary Figures 13–15 show the distributions of initializations in winning tickets pruned to various sparsity levels (layer-wise initialization histograms for winning tickets), which the authors use to argue that fortuitous initializations are especially critical at extreme sparsity; this supports that the original lottery-reset strategy yields superior retrainability at extreme compression compared to random reinitialization or continued training.
Fig. 13,Fig. 14,Fig. 15

Combine the absolute performance of original winning tickets at extreme $P_{m}$ (Tables 1 and 2) with the authors' reported comparisons and initialization analyses to conclude that, in these experiments, subnetworks found by the Lottery Ticket iterative-reset procedure consistently outperform the alternative pruning strategies in natural and adversarial accuracy at very high sparsity levels, demonstrating that preserving the original initialization is especially critical for successful retraining at extreme compression.
Table 1,Table 2,Fig. 13,Fig. 14,Fig. 15

State the experimental goal and the need for a reproducible protocol: the goal is to operationalize an evaluation that couples iterative pruning with adversarial training and to compare reset strategies so that the existence and properties of sparse, robust subnetworks can be assessed experimentally.

Define the three iterative pruning strategies evaluated, introducing notation used in the protocol: let $\mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ denote the distribution of initial parameters and let $m$ denote a binary mask of length $|\theta|$ with $m=1^{|\theta|}$ initially; define $P_{m} = \frac{\|m\|_0}{|\theta|}$ to be the fraction of weights remaining after pruning (sparsity). Then describe Strategy 1 (iterative pruning with resetting): after training the current masked network for $j$ iterations to parameters $m\odot\theta_j$, prune $s\%$ of parameters producing mask $m'$, and reset the remaining weights to their original initialization values $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ before the next training cycle; repeat until target sparsity is reached.

Describe Strategy 2 (iterative pruning with random reinitialization) using the same notation: after pruning to mask $m'$, reinitialize the remaining weights to fresh random draws $\theta_0' \sim \mathcal{D}_{\theta}$ (i.e., $\theta \leftarrow \theta_0'$) instead of resetting to the original $\theta_0$, and repeat training and pruning cycles until the desired sparsity $P_{m}$ is reached.

Describe Strategy 3 (iterative pruning with continued training) using the same notation: after pruning to mask $m'$, keep the current remaining parameters (do not reset or reinitialize), set $m \leftarrow m'$, and continue training; repeat until the desired $P_{m}$ is reached.

Specify the model architecture and the notation for model parameters used in all experiments: use a Lenet 300-100 multilayer perceptron, consisting of three fully connected layers of sizes 300, 100, and 10, resulting in $266{,}200$ trainable parameters; hidden layers use ReLU activations and the final output layer uses softmax; no biases are used in any layer.

Specify optimization and training schedule hyperparameters: use the Adam optimizer (Adam denotes the adaptive moment estimation optimizer) with learning rate $1.2\times 10^{-3}$, a batch size of $60$, and train for $50{,}000$ iterations per pruning iteration; pruning iterations are repeated for up to $20$ iterations as needed by the iterative pruning strategies.
[8]

Specify pruning rates per layer and how $P_{m}$ evolves under pruning: the first two layers have a pruning rate of $20\%$ per pruning iteration and the output layer has a pruning rate of $10\%$ per pruning iteration, so after each pruning iteration the mask $m$ is updated to remove these percentages of smallest-magnitude weights, updating $P_{m}$ accordingly.

Define adversarial attacks and their parameterization used to craft adversarial examples: use the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) which perturbs an input $\boldsymbol{x}$ by $\boldsymbol{\eta} = \epsilon\operatorname{sign}\left(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x},y)\right)$ with $\|\boldsymbol{\eta}\|_{\infty}<\epsilon$, and use Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) which iteratively updates $\boldsymbol{x}^{t+1} = \Pi_{\boldsymbol{x}+\mathcal{S}}\left(\boldsymbol{x}^t + \alpha\operatorname{sign}\left(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x},y)\right)\right)$. For both attacks in the experiments craft perturbations in the $\ell^{\infty}$ ball of $\epsilon=0.3$; for PGD use $10$ iterations and step size $\alpha=0.05$.
[6]
[14]

Specify adversarial training procedure and loss: adversarial training minimizes a mixture of categorical cross-entropy loss on natural examples and the same loss on adversarial examples using a $50/50$ split between natural and adversarial examples in each training batch.

Specify datasets and evaluation protocol: use MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion datasets, each with $60{,}000$ training and $10{,}000$ test examples, and further split training into $50{,}000$ training and $10{,}000$ validation examples; preprocess images by normalizing pixel values to $[0,1]$; evaluate models on natural and adversarial validation and test sets every $500$ training iterations.
[10]
[22]

Specify experiment averaging, software, and computational environment: average results over $5$ independent random trials and report standard deviation across trials; implement experiments in TensorFlow and generate adversarial attacks using the CleverHans library; experiments were executed on NVIDIA GeForce GTX TITAN X GPUs.
[1]
[15]

Summarize that combining the three pruning strategies with FGSM and PGD adversarial training under the stated hyperparameters, dataset splits, evaluation cadence, and averaging constitutes the reproducible experimental protocol used throughout the paper, thereby operationalizing iterative pruning with adversarial objectives for later comparisons.

open_questions.content: The study leaves several scientifically meaningful open issues. First, scalability: it remains unresolved whether the existence and properties of sparse, robust lottery tickets generalize to larger architectures and more complex vision datasets; extending the evaluation beyond Lenet 300-100 on MNIST Digits and MNIST Fashion is necessary to determine robustness-at-scale. Second, pruning structure and hardware compatibility: the experiments produce unstructured sparsity, which is not directly optimized for current libraries or hardware; it remains open how to obtain structured sparse, hardware-friendly robust subnetworks without sacrificing robustness. Third, algorithmic assumptions and theory: the pruning strategies assume small-magnitude weights are unimportant, a strong assumption whose validity for adversarial robustness is not proven; understanding when and why magnitude-based pruning preserves robustness is an open theoretical question. Fourth, attack and threat-model breadth: the paper did not evaluate all attack types (e.g., black-box attacks) and defers some comparative evaluations to future work, leaving the robustness of found tickets under a wider range of realistic threat models unresolved. Finally, computational cost: iterative pruning with adversarial training is computationally expensive, and it is open how to develop more efficient search or verification-friendly training procedures that retain robustness while reducing compute.
